clue.text: MENE-how God counted Belshazzar's kingdom

definitions.meaning: the first word of the writing on the wall in the Book of Daniel, which Daniel glosses as 'God hath counted thy kingdom'
Daniel reads the writing as saying the days of the Babylonian king's realm have been tallied and finished

explanation.walkthrough: In Daniel 5 the hand writes MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN at Belshazzar's feast; Daniel explains the first word as meaning the kingdom has been counted to its end.
explanation.definitionFit: MENE is the Aramaic word Daniel translates with this past participle, and it describes God tallying the kingdom's days.

clue.text: Jack's beanstalk eschewed by Peter Pan

definitions.meaning: the plant in the fairy tale that shoots up into the sky, an example of rising growth
the boy who never grew up avoided growing up, read as a split noun

explanation.walkthrough: The beanstalk is a growth upwards; Peter Pan refused to grow up, so he shunned 'up-growth'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means growth upward, which the beanstalk shows and which Peter Pan refused.

clue.text: Gay work, barring Newgate Gaol

parts.note: the ballad opera by John Gay, much of it set behind the bars of Newgate prison, where the highwayman Macheath is held

explanation.walkthrough: John Gay wrote the 1728 ballad opera; 'barring' points to prison bars in Newgate, the old London gaol where its hero is locked up.
explanation.definitionFit: John Gay's 1728 stage piece about thieves and highwaymen is the famous work meant.

clue.text: Made free with deer raised round the grassy tracts

indicators.note: the turned word goes round the other piece, enclosing it
in a down clue, a word raised is written from the bottom up, so it reads backwards

parts.note: taken as written
leas are meadows or grassy fields

explanation.surface: Freed deer go up round the meadows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' works only because this is a down entry: the deer is read upwards, giving a waterside plant, and 'round' wraps it about the meadows.
explanation.definitionFit: To liberate is to let go or set loose, as a prisoner is freed.

clue.text: Fish is a heavy one — it is implied

definitions.text: Fish is a heavy one — it is implied

parts.words: Fish is a heavy one — it is implied
parts.note: the saying 'drinks like a fish' implies that a fish takes in a great deal of liquid

explanation.walkthrough: Someone who drinks to excess 'drinks like a fish', so the fish is implied to be heavy at that.
explanation.definitionFit: One who imbibes alcohol, especially to excess, is a tippler.

clue.text: Must have influence, if turning up at a garage, so to demand …

definitions.text: at a garage, so to demand

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up reads the letters from the bottom, so the run is written backwards

parts.note: pull is influence, as in having pull with someone in power

explanation.surface: To get anywhere you need connections, and at the petrol station you ask for what follows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning up' reverses PULL plus IF together; the definition runs into the next clue, whose dots carry on with 'fuel'.
explanation.definitionFit: Asking a petrol-station attendant to top the tank is the request for a full tank.

clue.text: fuel, God willing, without hesitation

indicators.note: used in its old sense of outside, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: DV stands for Deo volente, Latin for God willing
er is the sound of a speaker hesitating

explanation.surface: Fuel ordered, God willing, without stumbling over the words.
explanation.walkthrough: DERV is British diesel road fuel. 'without' is used in its old sense of 'outside', not 'lacking'.
explanation.definitionFit: DERV, short for diesel-engined road vehicle, is diesel oil sold for lorries.

clue.text: A canny catcher perhaps ?

parts.note: catch-as-catch-can is a style of grappling, so one who practises it is a 'catch-can' fighter

explanation.walkthrough: 'Canny' reads as 'can-y', from catch-as-catch-can, a freestyle form of the sport of grappling.
explanation.definitionFit: A grappler who throws and pins opponents in the ring is a fighter in that sport.

clue.text: Albert's advice to abdication-minded Victoria, heard by Rudolph

indicators.note: the advice is spoken by Prince Albert, so we take its sound rather than its spelling

parts.note: a husband urging a queen tempted to give up the throne would say 'rein, dear': keep hold of the reins of government

explanation.surface: Prince Albert counsels a queen thinking of stepping down, and the words are overheard by someone called Rudolph.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rein, dear' said aloud matches the animal's name; Rudolph is the red-nosed member of Santa's team.
explanation.definitionFit: Rudolph is the most famous of Father Christmas's sleigh-pulling deer, an example of the species.

clue.text: A giant so eager to top another

parts.note: Gog is one of the two legendary giants, Gog and Magog, whose figures stand in London's Guildhall

explanation.surface: A giant keen to outdo a rival giant.
explanation.walkthrough: Gog is always named first in 'Gog and Magog', so he tops the other giant; the definition is the whole tail of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone keen and excited to outdo a rival is all eagerness, open-mouthed with anticipation.

clue.text: Musically episcopal clue for "Lawn"?

parts.note: a bishop wears sleeves of the fine linen called lawn, and a garden lawn is green, so the old English song title would serve as a clue for the word

explanation.walkthrough: Lawn is both a fine linen used for a bishop's sleeves (hence episcopal) and a stretch of green grass; the tune is a famous Tudor ballad.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of a well-known Tudor song describes green arms of a garment, the colour of grass and the cloth of bishops' sleeves.

clue.text: Madly (lacking money) cancel numbers of mortgages

indicators.note: letters going madly are thrown into a wild new order

parts.note: L, from the Latin libra, is the symbol for the pound, so it stands for money

explanation.surface: Wildly cancelling the figures on home loans when short of cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lacking' takes L (the pound sign) from CANCEL NUMBERS; 'Madly' rearranges the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Mortgages are legal claims on property, burdens that weigh down an estate.

clue.text: Eddies in the Westminster district, by Stevenson

parts.note: SW1 is the London postal district covering Westminster, with the 1 read as the letter I
RLS are the initials of Robert Louis Stevenson, author of Treasure Island

explanation.surface: Currents of water swirl through a part of London, beside a famous Scottish writer.
explanation.walkthrough: SW1 is the London postcode district that holds Parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: Eddies and whirling currents are twists of water, the same spinning motion.

clue.text: In particular East Place is in ruins

indicators.note: a place in ruins is broken up, so the letters of the two words are rebuilt

explanation.surface: A place in the east lies particularly ruined.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in ruins' looks like a description of the place but is the anagram signal; 'East' gives only its abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means special or notable, used in the phrase 'in particular' as an adverbial sense.

clue.text: Funereal wear for three masters, in a word ?

definitions.meaning: winding sheets in which the dead are wrapped for burial
the ropes bracing the masts of a sailing ship with three masts

explanation.walkthrough: The one word covers both senses: burial cloths and the side-rigging of a ship's masts.
explanation.definitionFit: Burial sheets are cloths wrapping a corpse; on a ship the same word names the standing rigging that steadies each mast.

clue.text: Bêtise is a fish, miscellaneous variety

parts.note: sole is a flatfish

indicators.note: a variety of something is another form of it, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A blunder is a fish of some miscellaneous sort.
explanation.walkthrough: A bêtise is French for a foolish remark or blunder. 'variety' acts on the abbreviation for miscellaneous, not the full word.
explanation.definitionFit: A grammatical blunder or social gaffe is a piece of stupidity, a foolish mistake.

clue.text: Music room

parts.note: the kind of music written for a small group in a private room rather than a concert hall, and also simply a room

explanation.walkthrough: The word means a room and also names the genre of music for small ensembles played in a room.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is an old synonym for a room, and it qualifies the music for small groups played in one.

clue.text: Its cases, not heard in court, are sometimes seen in the theatre

definitions.text: Its cases, not heard in court, are sometimes seen in the theatre

parts.words: Its cases, not heard in court, are sometimes seen in the theatre
parts.note: the cases are patients rather than lawsuits, and the theatre is the operating theatre

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cases' and 'theatre' look legal and dramatic but mean patients and an operating theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: A medical institution treats patients, whose cases go to surgery in its operating theatre.

clue.text: How to make emperor — look enraged ?

definitions.text: How to make emperor — look enraged ?

parts.words: How to make emperor — look enraged
parts.note: an emperor's look is imperial purple, and a face goes purple with rage

explanation.walkthrough: Imperial purple was the colour of emperors, and to go purple is to show fury.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to colour or flush with the royal dye of emperors, as a furious face reddens.

clue.text: Relatives produce a grand synonym for "buttocks

parts.note: G is short for grand, slang for a thousand
nates is the anatomical Latin for the buttocks

explanation.surface: Family members come up with a fancy word for a rude part of the body.
explanation.walkthrough: Agnates are relatives through the male line.
explanation.definitionFit: Kin descended from the same male ancestor are a kind of relation.

clue.text: Many happy returns — such a protracted birthday wish

definitions.meaning: lasting a long time, as in 'all the day long'
'...!' is what one wishes someone on a birthday, the same hope as 'many happy returns'

explanation.walkthrough: The adjective is known from 'the livelong day'; split in two it is the greeting 'Live long!'
explanation.definitionFit: As one word it means lasting tediously long; as two it is the toast for a long life.

clue.text: Banking system overturned in Square One

indicators.note: in a down clue, a thing overturned is upside down, so the word reads backwards

parts.note: giro is a system of bank transfer, as in the British National Giro
taken as written

explanation.surface: The banking system is overturned and we are back to the start.
explanation.walkthrough: Giro is a European system of direct bank transfer; 'overturned' suits a down entry, read from the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: Square one is the starting point, the place from which everything begins.

clue.text: One of the marks of corporal punishment ?

definitions.text: One of the marks of corporal punishment

parts.words: One of the marks of corporal punishment
parts.note: a weal left by a lash, and also one of the chevrons on a sleeve that mark a corporal's rank

explanation.walkthrough: 'Marks of corporal' are the two chevrons on an army corporal's sleeve; a lash also leaves a streak on the skin.
explanation.definitionFit: A weal from a whip is a long streak, and a corporal's rank badge is a chevron of the same name.

clue.text: China a bit too tricky for connubial life

indicators.note: something tricky is awkward to handle, so the letters of the four words are worked into a new order

explanation.surface: A married couple find the best china a little too delicate for daily use.
explanation.definitionFit: Living together as a married couple is the shared home life of husband and wife.

clue.text: 25's was a good one

parts.note: entry 25, a headland at the foot of Africa, bore a name meaning a good expectation

explanation.walkthrough: The headland at the southern tip of Africa is the Cape of Good ___; the cross-reference fills in the place.
explanation.definitionFit: A good expectation is an optimistic wish, the word that names the South African headland.

clue.text: Head of a one-time African colony

definitions.meaning: a headland, a point of land jutting into the sea
the British colony at the southern tip of Africa, later a province of South Africa

explanation.walkthrough: The Cape Colony was the British colony around Cape Town.
explanation.definitionFit: A headland is a promontory, and the former colony at Africa's southern tip took its name from such a promontory.

clue.text: County contains a very soft kind of stone

indicators.note: one word holding others within it, so the county wraps round the other letters

parts.note: a shire is an English county
pp, pianissimo, is the musical direction for very soft playing

explanation.surface: A county holds a deposit of very soft rock.
explanation.definitionFit: A blue gemstone, a variety of corundum, is a precious stone.

clue.text: Commercial travellers from a town near .Manchester ?

definitions.text: Commercial travellers from a town near .Manchester ?

parts.words: Commercial travellers from a town near .Manchester
parts.note: Sale is a town near Manchester, so its men are ..., the same letters as travelling sales representatives

explanation.walkthrough: Sale is a town in Greater Manchester; men from there are 'Sale's men'.
explanation.definitionFit: Commercial travellers were representatives who went from town to town selling goods.
